body: Denmark has standard white plates, yellow commercial plates, and unique "Parrot" plates with a yellow section on the left. Be cautious as the Netherlands, Luxembourg, and the UK use yellow plates for private vehicles.
Denmark is a generally flat country with wide, open fields. Suburban areas are typically open, while urban cores are more dense.
Denmark uses all-white road lines, and double middle lines are very common.
Outer road lines often consist of small white squares, which are a unique and identifying feature of Denmark.
Danish directional signs are very unique, often low to the ground and framed by pipes. They are either red and white or blue and white, with an arrow incorporated into the design.
Most Danish street names end in "vej," the Danish word for street. Street signs are typically blue with white text.
Denmark has a very recognizable white bollard with a yellow reflector and a dark orange stripe, which is unique to the country. A green variant can also be found.
The Danish language uses the special letters Æ, Ø, and Å. These letters are shared with other Nordic languages, so be cautious.
Much of Denmark's architecture consists of red brick with roofs of orange, dark brown, or black tiles. This style is also common in the Netherlands and Belgium.
Some rural houses in Denmark have thatched roofs. You can also sometimes find grey corrugated roofs.
Timber frame walls are a common feature of older or historical buildings in Denmark.
Signposts where the pipe frame is bent around the sign are unique to Denmark.
Denmark uses square (normal B-type) guardrails with no reflectors, a feature shared with only a few other European countries.
The Danish pedestrian sign has 5 stripes, with the first and fifth stripes uniquely touching the edge of the white triangle.
This unique sign, featuring a silhouette of a town, is found when entering urban areas in Denmark.
Danish bus stop signs are black and yellow. An older blue and white version may also be seen.
This red-and-white chevron is found in Denmark, often positioned low to the ground.
Standard utility poles are rare in Denmark; instead, large, towering overhead power lines are common, especially in the countryside.
Bicycle paths are commonly seen on the side of roads in Denmark, similar to the Netherlands and Belgium.
PostNord, the national postal service, uses unique red postal boxes.
The gas station brands Ingo, Ok, Uno-X, and Yx are common in Denmark and are each shared with one other Nordic country.
Rarely, you may see stone bollards with a red painted top near bicycle paths.
Denmark's road numbering system is ordered from east to west, making it a useful tool for region-guessing.
Ring roads (O1-O4) are special highways that encircle larger cities in Denmark.
Denmark's six regions each have a different bus transportation company with a unique color scheme and branding.
In addition to different bus companies, each of the six regions also has its own unique bus stop sign design.
Greenland is the world’s largest island and a part of Denmark. A separate guide for Greenland is available.
The Faroe Islands are an autonomous territory of Denmark located in the North Atlantic. A separate guide is available.
Bus stops on the island of Bornholm have a unique green, red, and white color scheme.
Green bicycle signs are a unique feature of the island of Bornholm.
The island of Læsø is known for its traditional "seaweed roofs" made from eelgrass.
The island of Anholt only has Generation 2 coverage, characterized by gloomy weather and sandy roadsides.
